entries.lesson_core_move: Apply the continuous-time Fourier series time-shifting property to convert coefficients for x(t) into coefficients for x(t - t0) by multiplying each c_k by e^{-jk omega0 t0} without recomputing the coefficient integral.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time-Shifting Property

blocks.text: When a periodic signal is shifted in time, its continuous-time Fourier series coefficients keep the same magnitudes and change only in phase. The phase change depends on the harmonic index, so the shift affects each coefficient in a controlled way instead of changing the whole spectrum.
Start with a periodic signal $x(t)$ whose CTFS coefficients are $c_k$. If the shifted signal is $y(t)=x(t-t_0)$, with $t_0>0$ meaning a delay, then the new coefficients are $d_k$.
The multiplier uses $k$, so each harmonic gets its own complex phase factor. The DC term is the special case $k=0$, where the multiplier becomes $1$ and $d_0=c_0$.

So a time shift changes coefficient phase, not coefficient magnitude. Once you know the original $c_k$, you can update the coefficients for a delay or an advance directly, without recomputing the Fourier integrals.

sections.section_title: Updating One Fourier Coefficient for a Delay

example_content.example_prompt: For a signal with coefficient $c_2=3e^{j\pi/4}$, find the corresponding coefficient $d_2$ for $y(t)=x(t-T_0/8)$.

explanation_blocks.text: This is a delay, so use the CTFS time-shifting property instead of recomputing the coefficient integral. The magnitude stays the same; only the phase changes.
Here the relevant harmonic is $k=2$, and the shift is $t_0=T_0/8$. Since a periodic signal satisfies $\omega_0T_0=2\pi$, the phase multiplier for this harmonic is $e^{-j\pi/2}$.
So the updated coefficient is $d_2=3e^{-j\pi/4}$. The coefficient magnitude is still $3$; only the phase has rotated.

sections.section_title: Updating a Coefficient List for x(t - t0)

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a delay, so update the whole coefficient list with the time-shifting property. Since $y(t)=x(t-T_0/4)$ and $\omega_0T_0=2\pi$, the common shift angle is $\omega_0t_0=\pi/2$.

explanation_blocks.latex: \begin{aligned} d_0 &= c_0 e^{-j0\omega_0t_0} = 2, \\ d_1 &= c_1 e^{-j1\omega_0t_0} = (1-j)e^{-j\pi/2} = -1-j, \\ d_2 &= c_2 e^{-j2\omega_0t_0} = 4e^{-j\pi} = -4 \end{aligned}

explanation_blocks.text: The DC term stays unchanged because its multiplier is $1$. The nonzero harmonics each pick up their own phase rotation from the same shift angle.
So the shifted coefficient list is $d_0=2$, $d_1=-1-j$, and $d_2=-4$. The result comes directly from the multiplier rule, without recomputing any Fourier integrals.

sections.section_title: Handling an Advance as a Negative Time Shift

example_content.example_prompt: For $c_3=2e^{-j\pi/3}$, find the $k=3$ coefficient of $y(t)=x(t+T_0/6)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the plus sign in $x(t+T_0/6)$. Rewrite it as $x(t-t_0)$ with $t_0=-T_0/6$, then apply the same CTFS time-shifting rule that you used for delays.

Now substitute the signed shift into $d_k=c_k e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}$. Since $\omega_0T_0=2\pi$, the phase for $k=3$ becomes $e^{-j3\omega_0(-T_0/6)}=e^{j\pi}$, which is a positive phase rotation because the shift is an advance.
So the coefficient is $d_3=2e^{j2\pi/3}$. The advance is handled by the negative value of $t_0$; the multiplier still does all the work, and the magnitude stays the same.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the harmonic-dependent phase change caused by a time shift by subtracting k omega0 t0 from each complex Fourier series coefficient phase while preserving the coefficient magnitudes.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Phase Change from Time Shifting

blocks.text: For a delay $x(t-t_0)$ with $t_0>0$, the complex Fourier series coefficient magnitudes stay fixed and only the phases change. The time shift is a harmonic-by-harmonic phase update, not a recomputation of the coefficient integral.

Write each original coefficient in polar form as $c_k = |c_k|e^{j\phi_k}$ so the phase change is visible directly. The shift leaves $|c_k|$ unchanged and changes only the angle attached to each harmonic index $k$.

The new phase is $\phi_k' = \phi_k-k\omega_0 t_0$, so higher harmonics rotate more because the phase subtraction is scaled by $k$. This is why the rule is harmonic-dependent even though the magnitude does not move.

For $k=0$, the multiplier is $e^0=1$, so the DC coefficient does not rotate at all. Use this coefficient-level rule whenever you want the shifted spectrum without recomputing Fourier integrals: keep the magnitudes, subtract $k\omega_0 t_0$ from each phase, and reuse the same notation for every harmonic.

sections.section_title: Phase Update for One Shifted Fourier Coefficient

example_content.example_prompt: Given $c_2 = 4e^{j\pi/6}$ for a periodic signal with fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$, find the new $k=2$ coefficient of $x(t-T_0/4)$ in polar form.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is one nonzero harmonic coefficient, $c_2 = 4e^{j\pi/6}$, so use the time-shift rule from the previous step: keep the magnitude and subtract the shift angle from the phase.
Here $t_0 = T_0/4$, so the phase change is $2\omega_0(T_0/4) = \omega_0T_0/2 = \pi/2$ because $\omega_0T_0 = 2\pi$. Subtract that angle from the original phase $\pi/6$.
So the shifted coefficient is $c_2' = 4e^{-j\pi/3}$. The magnitude stays $4$, and the only update is the phase subtraction by $k\omega_0t_0$.

sections.section_title: Phase Updates Across Multiple Harmonic Indices

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal has $c_0 = 3$, $c_1 = 2e^{j\pi/3}$, and $c_3 = e^{-j\pi/2}$. Find the shifted phases for $x(t-T_0/6)$ and write the new coefficient phases for $k=0,1,3$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a short coefficient list, so update each harmonic with the same rule $c_k' = c_k e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}$. Here $t_0 = T_0/6$, and the $k=0$ term stays fixed because no phase is subtracted when $k=0$.
That means the phase change is $k(\pi/3)$ for harmonic $k$, so the update is different at each index.

The $k=3$ result is the same as $\pi/2$ after wrapping by $2\pi$, so the shifted coefficients are $c_0' = 3$, $c_1' = 2$, and $c_3' = e^{j\pi/2}$. The magnitudes stay unchanged; only the phases move by the harmonic-dependent offset.

sections.section_title: Phase Sign for Delays and Advances

example_content.example_prompt: For the coefficient $c_1 = 5e^{-j\pi/4}$, compare the new phase for $x(t-T_0/8)$ with the new phase for $x(t+T_0/8)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is one coefficient with two opposite shifts. Use the same rule $c_k' = c_k e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}$, but note that a delay has $t_0>0$ and an advance has $t_0<0$. That sign change is what flips the phase direction.
Starting from $c_1 = 5e^{-j\pi/4}$, the delay uses $t_0 = T_0/8$, so the phase is reduced by $\pi/4$. The advance uses $t_0 = -T_0/8$, so the same subtraction rule turns into adding $\pi/4$.
So the delay gives $c_1' = 5e^{-j\pi/2}$ and the advance gives $c_1' = 5$. The magnitudes stay at $5$ in both cases; the sign of $t_0$ determines whether the phase moves down or up.

sections.section_title: Reading the Shifted Phase Spectrum

example_content.example_prompt: An original phase spectrum has all zero phases, and the shifted spectrum has $\phi'_0 = 0$, $\phi'_1 = -\pi/6$, $\phi'_2 = -\pi/3$, and $\phi'_3 = -\pi/2$. Identify the phase ramp and the time shift that produced it.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a completed phase spectrum, so read the phases by harmonic and check the change from one index to the next. Since the original phases are all zero, the shift shows up only as a linear phase ramp, and the magnitudes stay unchanged.
Each step between adjacent harmonics is the same, so compare the differences instead of treating the phases as separate numbers.
That constant step is $-\omega_0 t_0$, so $\omega_0 t_0 = \pi/6$ and $t_0 = T_0/12$. Because the phases get more negative as $k$ increases, the shift is a delay, and the ramp is $\phi'_k = -k\pi/6$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Recognize that time shifting a periodic signal leaves each Fourier series magnitude |c_k| unchanged because the time-shift multiplier only rotates coefficient phase.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Magnitude Spectrum Under Time Shifting

blocks.text: For one harmonic coefficient $c_k$ of a periodic signal, a time shift keeps the harmonic index fixed and changes only the coefficient phase. For $x(t-t_0)$, the shifted coefficient is $c_k' = c_k e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}$, so the first thing to recognize is the phase-rotation factor attached to the original coefficient.

The multiplier $e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}$ has unit magnitude, so it rotates $c_k$ in the complex plane without changing its length. That is the key cue: a time shift can move phase, but it cannot change the size of the coefficient.
So the magnitude spectrum stays the same for every harmonic index $k$, even though the phase spectrum changes. The shift changes where each coefficient points, not how tall each magnitude bar is.
Use this rule whenever a periodic signal is time shifted: multiply each coefficient by the phase factor, then read the magnitudes as unchanged.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Unit-Magnitude Time-Shift Multiplier

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal has Fourier coefficient $c_3 = 2 - 2j$. After the shift $x(t-t_0)$, the coefficient becomes $c_3' = c_3 e^{-j3\omega_0 t_0}$. Identify the multiplier's magnitude and the magnitude of $c_3'$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the factor multiplying $c_3$ in the shifted coefficient. For $x(t-t_0)$, the shift does not change the harmonic index; it appends the multiplier $e^{-j3\omega_0 t_0}$ to the original coefficient.
Because $e^{-j3\omega_0 t_0}$ is a complex exponential, its magnitude is $1$. So the shift changes phase only, not coefficient size.
Now compute the original magnitude: $|c_3| = |2-2j| = \sqrt{2^2+(-2)^2} = 2\sqrt{2}$. Since the multiplier has unit magnitude, the shifted coefficient keeps that same magnitude.
So the multiplier is unit-magnitude, and the shifted coefficient has magnitude $2\sqrt{2}$. The phase changes, but the magnitude spectrum height does not.

sections.section_title: Finding Magnitudes After a Time Shift

example_content.example_prompt: A signal has coefficients $c_0 = 2$, $c_1 = 1 - j$, and $c_2 = -3j$. After the shift $x(t-t_0)$, determine the shifted magnitudes $|c_0'|$, $|c_1'|$, and $|c_2'|$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the time-shift factor on each coefficient. A shift leaves the coefficient list in place and multiplies each harmonic by a complex exponential with magnitude $1$, so the magnitudes should match the original list.

explanation_blocks.latex: c_0' = c_0,\qquad c_1' = c_1 e^{-j\omega_0 t_0},\qquad c_2' = c_2 e^{-j2\omega_0 t_0}

explanation_blocks.text: Start with the original magnitudes: $|c_0| = |2| = 2$, $|c_1| = |1-j| = \sqrt{1^2+(-1)^2} = \sqrt{2}$, and $|c_2| = |-3j| = 3$.
So the shifted magnitude list is identical to the original one: the Fourier-series spectrum heights do not change under time shifting. Only the phases rotate.

sections.section_title: Comparing Original and Shifted Magnitude Spectra

example_content.example_prompt: The original magnitude spectrum is $\{|c_0|, |c_1|, |c_2|\} = \{4, 1, 2\}$. After shifting the signal to $x(t-t_0)$, which magnitude spectrum is correct?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the full magnitude list, not the complex coefficients. A time shift changes each coefficient by a unit-magnitude factor, so each entry in the spectrum keeps its height.
Apply the shift rule term by term: $|c_0'| = |c_0| = 4$, $|c_1'| = |c_1| = 1$, and $|c_2'| = |c_2| = 2$.
So the correct shifted magnitude spectrum is the same ordered list as the original one. The coefficients rotate in phase, but the spectrum heights do not move or scale.

sections.section_title: Distinguishing Magnitude Invariance from Phase Rotation

example_content.example_prompt: A student says the magnitude spectrum must change because $c_k' = c_k e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}$. Decide what changes and what stays the same for $x(t-t_0)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the update rule itself. A time shift does not rewrite the coefficient list; it multiplies each $c_k$ by a complex exponential that depends on $k$, so the only question is whether that multiplier changes magnitude or only phase.
The exponential factor has magnitude $1$, so it cannot change $|c_k|$. It only rotates the phase by an amount that depends on $k$ and the shift $t_0$.
So the student's claim is false. A time shift changes phase, not magnitude: the magnitude spectrum stays fixed while the phase spectrum rotates.

entries.lesson_core_move: Update the Fourier series coefficients of a vertically shifted periodic signal by adding the constant offset to the DC coefficient and leaving every nonzero harmonic coefficient unchanged.

sections.section_title: Introduction to DC Adjustment from Vertical Shifting

blocks.text: Start from a periodic signal with known trigonometric Fourier coefficients. In this form, $a_0$ is the constant or DC term, so it is the coefficient to watch when the signal is shifted vertically.
Now form the vertically shifted signal $x_{\text{new}}(t)=x(t)+c$. The added constant $c$ folds into the constant term, while the harmonic terms stay attached to the same cosine and sine components.

So the update rule is: add $c$ to the DC coefficient and leave every coefficient with $n\ge 1$ unchanged. Later examples can reuse this exact notation as $a_0^{\text{new}}=a_0+c$, $a_n^{\text{new}}=a_n$, and $b_n^{\text{new}}=b_n$.

sections.section_title: Adding a Positive Offset to the DC Coefficient

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal has trigonometric Fourier coefficients $a_0=2$, $a_1=-1$, $b_1=4$, $a_2=0$, and $b_2=-3$. The signal is shifted upward by $5$. Update the coefficient set.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a vertical shift upward by $5$, so use the DC-update rule $a_0^{\text{new}}=a_0+c$. Read the original coefficient list first, then apply the offset only to $a_0$.

The harmonic coefficients stay fixed: $a_1^{\text{new}}=-1$, $b_1^{\text{new}}=4$, $a_2^{\text{new}}=0$, and $b_2^{\text{new}}=-3$. So the updated coefficient set is the original list with only the DC term changed.

sections.section_title: Applying a Negative Offset to the DC Coefficient

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal has coefficients $a_0=9$, $a_1=2$, $b_1=-1$, $a_2=-4$, and $b_2=6$. The signal is shifted downward by $3$. Update the coefficient set.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a vertical shift downward by $3$, so treat the shift as $c=-3$ and use the same DC-update rule $a_0^{\text{new}}=a_0+c$. Only the constant term should move.

The harmonic coefficients stay fixed: $a_1^{\text{new}}=2$, $b_1^{\text{new}}=-1$, $a_2^{\text{new}}=-4$, and $b_2^{\text{new}}=6$. So the updated coefficient set keeps every nonzero harmonic term unchanged.

sections.section_title: Keeping Nonzero Harmonic Coefficients Unchanged

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal is shifted upward by $2$. The original coefficients are $a_0=-1$, $a_1=5$, $b_1=0$, $a_2=-2$, and $b_2=4$. Identify which coefficients change and state the updated set.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a vertical shift upward by $2$, so treat it as $c=2$ and use the same DC-update rule $a_0^{\text{new}}=a_0+c$. The only coefficient that changes is the constant term.

Copy the harmonic coefficients exactly as written: $a_1^{\text{new}}=5$, $b_1^{\text{new}}=0$, $a_2^{\text{new}}=-2$, and $b_2^{\text{new}}=4$. The zero harmonic term stays zero, and every nonzero harmonic term stays unchanged.

sections.section_title: Updating a Complete Fourier Coefficient Set After a Vertical Shift

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal has coefficients $a_0=\tfrac{3}{2}$, $a_1=-2$, $b_1=1$, $a_2=0$, $b_2=-\tfrac{5}{2}$, $a_3=4$, and $b_3=3$. The signal is shifted upward by $\tfrac{7}{2}$. Update the full coefficient set and rewrite the trigonometric Fourier series.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a vertical shift upward by $\tfrac{7}{2}$, so use the DC-update rule $a_0^{\text{new}}=a_0+c$. Apply the offset to the constant term first, then carry every harmonic coefficient forward unchanged.

Now copy the harmonic coefficients exactly: $a_1^{\text{new}}=-2$, $b_1^{\text{new}}=1$, $a_2^{\text{new}}=0$, $b_2^{\text{new}}=-\tfrac{5}{2}$, $a_3^{\text{new}}=4$, and $b_3^{\text{new}}=3$. Since the series uses $a_0^{\text{new}}/2$, the new constant term in the rewritten series is $\tfrac{5}{2}$.

explanation_blocks.latex: a_0^{\text{new}}=5,\qquad a_1^{\text{new}}=-2,\qquad b_1^{\text{new}}=1,\qquad a_2^{\text{new}}=0,\qquad b_2^{\text{new}}=-\tfrac{5}{2},\qquad a_3^{\text{new}}=4,\qquad b_3^{\text{new}}=3
x_{\text{shifted}}(t)=\tfrac{5}{2}-2\cos(\omega_0 t)+\sin(\omega_0 t)+0\cos(2\omega_0 t)-\tfrac{5}{2}\sin(2\omega_0 t)+4\cos(3\omega_0 t)+3\sin(3\omega_0 t)

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert the Fourier series coefficients of x(t) to those of x(-t) by replacing each harmonic coefficient with the coefficient at the opposite index and interpreting the spectra as harmonic-index reversals.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time-Reversal Property

blocks.text: For the complex Fourier series, time reversal is a harmonic-index reversal. The coefficient at harmonic $k$ in $x(-t)$ comes from the coefficient at harmonic $-k$ in $x(t)$, so the coefficient sequence is read backward around $k=0$.
Start by substituting $-t$ into the series. This changes the sign in each exponential, but it does not change the coefficient values themselves.
Now reindex the sum so the exponent returns to the standard positive-$k$ form. That reindexing gives $C_k^{x(-t)} = C_{-k}^{x(t)}$.

The $k=0$ coefficient stays fixed, and each matched pair of harmonics $k$ and $-k$ swaps sides. So the magnitude and phase spectra of $x(-t)$ are mirror images of those of $x(t)$ across harmonic index $0$.

sections.section_title: Mapping One Fourier Series Coefficient Under Time Reversal

example_content.example_prompt: Given a coefficient table for $x(t)$ with entries around $k=0$, such as $C_{-2}=1+j$, $C_{-1}=2$, $C_0=3$, $C_1=2-j$, and $C_2=1-j$, determine $C_2$ for $x(-t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a coefficient table centered at $k=0$. For time reversal, the coefficient at harmonic $k$ in $x(-t)$ comes from the coefficient at harmonic $-k$ in $x(t)$.
From the given table, the opposite-index coefficient is $C_{-2}=1+j$. Keep that value unchanged and assign it to the target index.
So the reversed signal uses the same coefficient value at the mirrored harmonic index: the lookup changes from $-2$ to $2$, but the coefficient itself does not change.

sections.section_title: Reversing a Full Fourier Coefficient Sequence

example_content.example_prompt: Given the coefficient list for $x(t)$ with the five harmonics $k=-2,-1,0,1,2$, write the full coefficient list for $x(-t)$ in the same index convention.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a finite coefficient list centered at $k=0$. Time reversal does not change the coefficient values; it reverses the harmonic order around $0$.
Read the original list from most negative to most positive. Then move each coefficient to the opposite harmonic index: $-2$ swaps with $2$, $-1$ swaps with $1$, and $0$ stays fixed.
So the full coefficient list for $x(-t)$ is the same list read backward around $0$. The center term stays in place, and the left and right sides swap positions.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Magnitude Spectrum After Time Reversal

example_content.example_prompt: Given the magnitude table $|C_{-2}|=5$, $|C_{-1}|=3$, $|C_0|=2$, $|C_1|=1$, and $|C_2|=4$ for $x(t)$, identify the magnitude table for $x(-t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a magnitude table indexed by harmonic number $k$. For time reversal, the magnitude values do not change; only the index order mirrors about $0$.
Mirror the index order about $0$: $-2$ pairs with $2$, $-1$ pairs with $1$, and $0$ stays fixed. Keep each magnitude value attached to the opposite index instead of recomputing it.
So the magnitude spectrum of $x(-t)$ is the left-right mirror of the magnitude spectrum of $x(t)$: the values read $4, 1, 2, 3, 5$ from $k=-2$ to $k=2$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Phase Spectrum After Time Reversal

example_content.example_prompt: Given the phase table $\angle C_{-2}=-\pi/2$, $\angle C_{-1}=0$, $\angle C_0=\pi/6$, $\angle C_1=\pi/3$, and $\angle C_2=-\pi/4$ for $x(t)$, identify the phase table for $x(-t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a phase table indexed by harmonic number $k$. For time reversal, the phase values stay the same while the index order mirrors about $0$.
Mirror the index order about $0$: $-2$ pairs with $2$, $-1$ pairs with $1$, and $0$ stays fixed. Move each phase value to the opposite index instead of changing the phase value itself.

explanation_blocks.latex: \angle C_{-2}^{x(-t)}=\angle C_2^{x(t)}=-\pi/4,\quad \angle C_{-1}^{x(-t)}=\angle C_1^{x(t)}=\pi/3,\quad \angle C_0^{x(-t)}=\angle C_0^{x(t)}=\pi/6,\quad \angle C_1^{x(-t)}=\angle C_{-1}^{x(t)}=0,\quad \angle C_2^{x(-t)}=\angle C_{-2}^{x(t)}=-\pi/2

explanation_blocks.text: So the phase spectrum of $x(-t)$ is the left-right mirror of the phase spectrum of $x(t)$: read from $k=-2$ to $k=2$, the phases are $-\pi/4$, $\pi/3$, $\pi/6$, $0$, and $-\pi/2$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Determine how time scaling x(at) changes the fundamental period and angular frequency while reusing the original Fourier coefficient sequence with any sign-induced index reversal.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time-Scaling Property

blocks.text: When a periodic signal is written as $y(t)=x(at)$, the key object to track is the scale factor $a$ acting on the original signal $x(t)$. Start from $x(t)$ with fundamental period $T_0$ and Fourier coefficients $c_k$.

This means time compression or expansion changes the fundamental period but does not create a new coefficient sequence. The new fundamental angular frequency follows the same rescaling on the frequency grid, so a smaller period corresponds to a larger angular frequency and a larger period corresponds to a smaller angular frequency.
For $a>0$, the harmonic index $k$ keeps the same coefficient $c_k$ on the new frequency grid. The values stay in the same order; only the period and angular spacing change.

For $a<0$, the sign of $a$ adds time reversal, so the coefficient at harmonic index $k$ becomes $c_{-k}$. The period and angular frequency still use $|a|$, but the index direction flips because the signal has been reversed in time.

So the rule to remember is: time scaling changes the period and fundamental angular frequency, while positive scaling reuses the same coefficient sequence and negative scaling reverses the harmonic indices.

sections.section_title: Finding the New Period After Time Scaling

example_content.example_prompt: If $x(t)$ has fundamental period $T_0=12$, find the fundamental period of $y(t)=x(3t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a periodic signal written as $y(t)=x(at)$. Here the scaling factor is $a=3$, so the goal is to apply the period rule from the introduction rather than recompute anything from scratch.
Now substitute the original period and the scale factor: $T_y=12/|3|$. Since $|3|=3$, the new signal is compressed in time by a factor of $3$, so its period must shrink by the same factor.
So the fundamental period of $y(t)=x(3t)$ is $4$. The result stays positive because period depends on $|a|$, even though the signal itself has been time-compressed.

sections.section_title: Finding the New Fundamental Angular Frequency After Time Scaling

example_content.example_prompt: If $x(t)$ has fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0=5$ rad/s, find the fundamental angular frequency of $y(t)=x(2t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is still the time-scaling form $y(t)=x(at)$, but now we read the frequency side of the property instead of the period side. For $y(t)=x(2t)$, the scaling factor is $a=2$ and the original fundamental angular frequency is $\omega_0=5$ rad/s.
Now substitute the values: $\omega_y=|2|(5)$. Because $|2|=2$, the frequency grid stretches by a factor of $2$ when the signal is compressed in time, so the fundamental angular frequency doubles.

So the new fundamental angular frequency is $10$ rad/s. This is the frequency-side counterpart of the shorter period from the previous example: time compression shrinks the period and increases the fundamental angular frequency by the same factor.

sections.section_title: Reusing Coefficients for Positive Time Scaling

example_content.example_prompt: Let $x(t)$ have CTFS coefficients $c_k$ with fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$. For $y(t)=x(2t)$, identify $d_k$ and the new fundamental angular frequency.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a positive time scaling in CTFS form. For $y(t)=x(2t)$, the scaling factor is $a=2$, so we keep the original coefficient sequence but read it on a new frequency grid with doubled spacing.
Rewrite the exponent as $jk(2\omega_0)t$. That identifies the new fundamental angular frequency as $2\omega_0$, which is exactly what positive time compression should do to the harmonic spacing.
Reading this against the standard CTFS form shows that $d_k=c_k$ for every harmonic index $k$ and $\omega_y=2\omega_0$. Positive scaling changes the frequency grid, not the coefficient values.

sections.section_title: Applying Index Reversal for Negative Time Scaling

example_content.example_prompt: Let $x(t)$ have coefficients $c_k$. For $y(t)=x(-2t)$, state the new fundamental angular frequency and the coefficient rule for $d_k$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the same time-scaling form, but the negative sign means the frequency-grid update must be paired with time reversal. For $y(t)=x(-2t)$, separate the operation into scaling by $2$ and reversing time.
Use $|a|$ for the frequency change, so the new fundamental angular frequency is $2\omega_0$. The negative sign does not change the size of the frequency step; it only flips the index direction.
So the new fundamental angular frequency is $2\omega_0$ and the coefficient rule is $d_k=c_{-k}$. Negative scaling changes the index direction, not the coefficient values themselves.

entries.lesson_core_move: Infer the negative-harmonic Fourier series coefficients of a real periodic signal from the positive-harmonic coefficients using conjugate symmetry, then translate the relationship into even magnitude and odd phase spectra.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Conjugate Symmetry for Real Signals

blocks.text: For a real periodic signal, the complex Fourier series coefficients come in conjugate pairs. The negative-harmonic side is not independent: once the positive-harmonic coefficients are known, the matching negative-harmonic coefficients are determined by the real-signal condition.

The smallest complete case is one harmonic pair such as $c_1$ and $c_{-1}$, together with the DC term $c_0$. If the signal is real, then $c_{-1}$ is the complex conjugate of $c_1$, and $c_0$ stays real, so the learner does not recompute the coefficient integral for the negative side.

In rectangular form, conjugation keeps the real part and flips the sign of the imaginary part. So if $c_k=a_k+j b_k$, then the matching negative-harmonic coefficient is $c_{-k}=a_k-j b_k$. That is the same rule written component by component.

This is why the magnitude spectrum is even in $k$, while the phase spectrum is odd in $k$. For a real periodic signal, one side of the spectrum determines the other, and $c_0$ remains the real center term.

sections.section_title: Relating Positive and Negative Fourier Series Coefficients

example_content.example_prompt: A real periodic signal has $c_2 = 3 - 4j$. Find $c_{-2}$ and confirm what the rule says about the pair.

explanation_blocks.text: A real periodic signal uses the conjugate-symmetry rule from the previous section, so the negative-harmonic coefficient is determined by the positive-harmonic coefficient. The cue here is a real signal with a known positive-index coefficient, which means the matching negative-index coefficient is not independent.

For the concrete pair in this example, the given coefficient is $c_2 = 3 - 4j$. The matching negative-harmonic coefficient is its complex conjugate, so we switch the sign of the imaginary part and keep the real part the same.
This pair has the same magnitude and opposite phase, which is exactly what conjugate symmetry predicts for a real periodic signal. If a DC term $c_0$ were present, it would remain real as well.

sections.section_title: Inferring Missing Negative-Harmonic Coefficients

example_content.example_prompt: A coefficient table gives $c_0 = 4$, $c_1 = 2 - j$, and $c_3 = -1 + 2j$. Fill in the missing negative-harmonic coefficients.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a real periodic signal with several known positive-harmonic coefficients. That means each missing negative-harmonic entry comes from mirroring the known positive side with conjugation, one index at a time.
Start with $c_1 = 2 - j$. The matching negative coefficient is its complex conjugate, so the real part stays the same and the imaginary part changes sign.
Do the same for $c_3 = -1 + 2j$. Apply the same rule again instead of inventing a new pattern.
Keep $c_0 = 4$ unchanged because the DC coefficient of a real signal is real. The completed table now has consistent pairs across $\pm 1$ and $\pm 3$.

sections.section_title: Finding Even Magnitude Symmetry

example_content.example_prompt: A real periodic signal has $c_2 = 3 - 4j$ and $c_{-2} = 3 + 4j$. Find $|c_2|$ and explain why the magnitude spectrum is even.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a conjugate pair from a real signal. For magnitude, conjugates give the same absolute value, so the task is to compute one magnitude and reuse it on the negative side.
For $c_2 = 3 - 4j$, take the absolute value of the complex number. The magnitude is $|c_2| = 5$.
Because $c_{-2} = 3 + 4j$ is the conjugate of $c_2$, its magnitude is the same. That is the even-magnitude pattern across $+2$ and $-2$. A DC term, if present, stays real and one-sided.

sections.section_title: Finding Odd Phase Symmetry

example_content.example_prompt: A real periodic signal has $c_2 = 1 + j$. If the phase of $c_2$ is $45$ degrees, what is the phase of $c_{-2}$?

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a real-signal conjugate pair, but the question is asking for phase. For a conjugate pair, the negative-harmonic phase is the negative of the positive-harmonic phase, while the magnitude stays the same as a check.
Here the positive-harmonic phase is $45$ degrees, so flip the sign for the negative-harmonic coefficient.
The magnitude is unchanged, so the phase result is consistent with the same conjugate pair. That is the odd-phase symmetry across $+2$ and $-2$.

sections.section_title: Using Conjugate Symmetry to Complete a Spectrum

example_content.example_prompt: A real periodic signal gives $c_0 = 2$, $c_1 = 1 - j$, and $c_2 = -2j$. Which completed coefficient table and symmetry statement are correct?

explanation_blocks.text: This is a spectrum-completion task. The cue is a real periodic signal with a partial coefficient table, so the missing negative-side entries come from conjugating each positive-side coefficient, and the magnitude and phase symmetries come from the same mirrored pairs.
Mirror each given positive-harmonic coefficient: $c_1 = 1 - j$ becomes $c_{-1} = 1 + j$, and $c_2 = -2j$ becomes $c_{-2} = 2j$. Keep $c_0 = 2$ unchanged.

The completed spectrum shows the same magnitudes on each mirrored pair and opposite phase signs on each mirrored pair. That is the direct combination of even magnitude symmetry and odd phase symmetry.

entries.lesson_title: Using Properties Instead of Recomputing Integrals
entries.lesson_core_move: Select and apply the appropriate Fourier series property to convert known coefficients into coefficients for a shifted, scaled, reversed, vertically shifted, or real-signal variant without recomputing the coefficient integral.

sections.lesson_title: Using Properties Instead of Recomputing Integrals
sections.section_title: Introduction to Using Properties Instead of Recomputing Integrals

blocks.text: You already know the Fourier-series property formulas. In this lesson, the job is not to re-integrate; it is to inspect a transformed periodic signal with known $c_k$ and reuse the matching property or property chain to update the coefficients directly.

Scan the signal statement for the cue: time shift, time scaling, time reversal, vertical offset, or real-signal symmetry. If the signal has more than one change, chain the matching properties in the same order as the transformations instead of starting over with the coefficient integral.

For a single shift, every harmonic coefficient changes by the corresponding phase rule; for a vertical shift, only the DC term changes. When the signal is real, use symmetry to fill the negative indices instead of recomputing them.

Use the quick check: ask what changes in $c_k$, what changes only in $c_0$, and when negative coefficients come from symmetry. If you can answer those three questions, you can update the coefficients directly and avoid recomputing the coefficient integral.

sections.lesson_title: Using Properties Instead of Recomputing Integrals
sections.section_title: Selecting the Property from a Transformed Signal

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal $x(t)$ has known coefficients $c_k$. The new signal is $y(t)=x(-t)$. Decide which Fourier-series property applies and state how the coefficient indices change.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is the minus sign inside the argument: $y(t)=x(-t)$. That tells you the signal has been time-reversed, so the property to select is the time-reversal property rather than a shift or a scaling.

Read that rule as an index swap: the new coefficient at harmonic $k$ is the old coefficient at harmonic $-k$. Because this example contains only time reversal, you stop here and do not recompute the coefficient integral.

sections.lesson_title: Using Properties Instead of Recomputing Integrals
sections.section_title: Updating Known Coefficients with One Fourier Series Property

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal $x(t)$ has coefficients $c_k$. Find the coefficients of $y(t)=x(t-t_0)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the delay inside $y(t)=x(t-t_0)$. That tells you to use the time-shift property, so each Fourier-series coefficient keeps its magnitude and picks up a harmonic-dependent phase factor.

So the update is coefficient-by-coefficient: multiply every $c_k$ by $e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}$ and leave the magnitudes unchanged. The $k=0$ term stays the same, and no coefficient integral is recomputed.

sections.lesson_title: Using Properties Instead of Recomputing Integrals
sections.section_title: Combining a Time Shift with a Vertical Shift

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal $x(t)$ has coefficients $c_k$. Find the coefficients of $y(t)=x(t-t_0)+A$.

explanation_blocks.text: The delay inside $x(t-t_0)$ is the first cue. Apply the time-shift property to the known coefficients before you handle the constant offset.
Then add the vertical shift. The constant $A$ changes only the DC term, so $d_0=\tilde c_0+A=c_0+A$ while every $k\neq 0$ coefficient stays equal to the time-shifted value.

The update is ordered and local: first update every coefficient by the time-shift rule, then change only the DC term by the vertical offset. That keeps the combined transformation from turning into a recomputation.

sections.lesson_title: Using Properties Instead of Recomputing Integrals
sections.section_title: Combining Time Reversal with Time Scaling

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal $x(t)$ has coefficients $c_k$ and period $T$. Determine the coefficients and new fundamental period of $y(t)=x(-2t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the negative scale in $x(-2t)$. Treat it as a time reversal together with a factor-2 compression of the time axis.
Once the new period is fixed, use the reversal rule on the coefficient sequence. The harmonic index order flips, so the coefficient at index $k$ comes from the old coefficient at $-k$.
So the update is complete: halve the period, double the fundamental angular frequency, and read the coefficient list backward. No coefficient integral is recomputed.

sections.lesson_title: Using Properties Instead of Recomputing Integrals
sections.section_title: Using Conjugate Symmetry to Complete Coefficient Updates

example_content.example_prompt: A real periodic signal has updated positive-harmonic coefficients after a transformation. Use conjugate symmetry to determine the missing negative-index coefficients and complete the spectrum.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the signal is real after the transformation. That means the completed Fourier-series coefficients must satisfy conjugate symmetry.
So after you update the positive harmonics, fill each missing negative coefficient by conjugating the matching positive one. Leave the DC term real, and do not recompute any integrals.
That completes the spectrum directly from the known positive side: mirror the indices, apply conjugation, and keep the zero-frequency term real.
